column4: The ban on nullifying charity through reminders and injury completes 2:262–263: a materially open hand is still hard if it humiliates its recipient afterward.
After refusing to drive believers away in 11:29, Noah asks who could protect him from God if he did so, making non-expulsion a matter of accountability rather than courtesy.
Between the ban on expulsion and the greeting of peace, elites ask whether these low-status believers are really those God favored; the ayah identifies the contempt that produces the hard dismissal.
The command “Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed” identifies the violent addressee before 20:44 requires gentle speech, showing that softness is deliberate even toward tyranny.
After evil is repelled with what is better in 41:34, this response is said to be received only by the patient and greatly fortunate; patient restraint is what sustains the gentle answer.
The patience preferred in 16:126 is possible only through God, and the Prophet must not grieve or feel constricted by opponents' schemes.
The giver of 92:5 also affirms the finest promise; that receptive assent is the inward yielding that leads to ease in 92:7.
The self-sufficient withholder denies the finest promise, supplying the inward refusal that leads to the difficult path in 92:10.
After forbidding the Prophet's hurried tongue in 75:16, God assumes responsibility for collecting and reciting the revelation, replacing anxious grasping with trustful reception.
Once God recites the revelation, the Prophet is to follow its recitation; measured following is the positive movement opposite haste.
The Prophet must patiently await his Lord's judgment and not repeat Jonah's distressed reaction; this prepares for the preserving divine favor in 68:49.
A town secure and tranquil, with abundant provision, denies God's favors and loses its ease; the named blessing root is tested through gratitude rather than possession.
The Prophet is told to glorify God before sunrise, before sunset, and during the night so that he may be satisfied; daily light and darkness culminate in the same رضى promised in 93:5.
فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا is a direct divine assurance to the Prophet that ease accompanies hardship, close to the section's yielding and restful semantic field.
The repeated assurance that ease accompanies hardship makes gentleness and facilitation emphatic rather than incidental.
God explicitly intends ease for people and does not intend hardship in the fasting law, stating the divine preference that the section perceives through its soft roots.
God wishes to lighten the human burden because humanity was created weak, a direct formulation of mercifully adjusted pressure.
God has placed no constricting hardship in religion; the ayah makes non-oppressive religious obligation part of Abraham's inherited path.
The invitation to lend generously is followed by وَاللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْسُطُ; constriction and expansion become explicit divine “holds” around human giving.
Immediately after the measured-hand command of 17:29, the Lord expands and restricts provision with full knowledge, distinguishing divine measure from human stinginess.
The One holding the keys of heaven and earth expands and restricts provision, assigning ultimate opening and tightening to divine knowledge.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily but keep a measured middle course, giving the open hand a disciplined balance.
When people are called to spend, some withhold; the ayah says the withholder is withholding only from himself, exposing the closed hand's self-defeat.
The Helpers prefer others even while needy themselves, and success belongs to those protected from the soul's stinginess; generous reception overcomes the inner hard grip.
Listening, obeying, and spending are joined to protection from the soul's stinginess, again locating the obstruction to giving within the self.
The God-conscious spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people, uniting an open hand with control of the impulse to strike back.
Those who avoid grave wrongs forgive when angered, making release at the moment of provocation a mark of faithful character.
Patient endurance and forgiveness are described as matters of firm resolve, elevating gentle release above reactive hardness.
God does not love public evil speech, except from one who has been wronged; the exception draws a precise boundary around restraint of the harsh tongue.
The Prophet must not obey a habitual, contemptible swearer; the passage begins a portrait of corrosive speech and hard character.
The same figure is a fault-finder who moves about spreading slander, specifying the rebuking tongue as a settled social practice.
He obstructs good, transgresses, and sins, joining the harmful tongue to a hand that prevents benefit from reaching others.
His character is further marked as cruel and ignoble, completing the passage's concentrated opposite to gentleness.
A good word is likened to a good tree with firm root and high branches, making constructive speech a living, sheltering presence.
The good tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission, showing the ongoing yield produced by the good word of 14:24.
An evil word is like an uprooted tree with no stability, a direct reversal of the gentle word's rooted and fruitful effect.
The best speech belongs to one who calls to God, acts rightly, and declares submission, defining excellence of speech through invitation rather than rebuke.
The saved are guided to wholesome speech and to the path of the Praiseworthy, placing the section's guidance root directly beside good words.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are precisely those God has guided, joining verbal discernment to the named guidance root.
Believers are commanded to fear God and speak a straight, sound word, another positive discipline placed on the tongue.
Those who fear leaving vulnerable children behind must fear God and speak a sound word, linking concern for weak offspring with responsible speech.
Believers must make room for one another in gatherings and rise when asked; social space is handled through accommodation rather than status pressure.
Affliction should have brought humility, but hearts hardened instead; the ayah identifies inward hardness as resistance to corrective mercy.
Satanic suggestion becomes a trial for diseased and hardened hearts, again making hardness the condition that distorts reception.
Those given knowledge recognize the truth and their hearts become humbly receptive to it, supplying the softened counterpart to 22:53.
Woe is pronounced on hearts hardened against God's remembrance, preparing the explicit softening of skins and hearts in 39:23.
God burdens no soul beyond its capacity, expressing a divine hold calibrated to the weakness of the person held.
The Messenger relieves people of their burdens and the shackles upon them, turning prophetic guidance into bodily and legal release.
There is no compulsion in religion, yet the believer grasps the firmest handhold; secure holding is distinguished from coercive force in one ayah.
If hearers turn away, the Prophet has not been sent as their guardian; his task is conveyance, not controlling their response.
The Prophet is neither appointed guardian over idolaters nor manager of them, preparing the non-abusive speech boundary of 6:108.
After obedience to the Messenger is tied to obedience to God, the Prophet is told he has not been sent as a guardian over those who turn away.
The Prophet receives the Book for people, but whoever strays does so against himself and the Prophet is not their manager.
Noah asks whether he could force divine mercy upon unwilling hearers, rejecting coercion in the same dispute where elites want poor believers expelled.
After Pharaoh claims qahr in 7:127, Moses tells his people to seek God's help and remain patient because the earth belongs to God, relocating mastery from tyrant to Lord.
Pharaoh answers Moses' proclamation by threatening prison, a coercive verbal response that exposes the regime addressed with gentle speech.
Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord, making explicit the usurped supremacy behind his human qahr.
God seizes Pharaoh in exemplary punishment for his latter and former offenses, contrasting the tyrant's grasp with final divine seizure.
Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the population, weakens a group, and slaughters its sons; the ayah unfolds domination plus degradation, the section's definition of qahr.
Israel is rescued from Pharaoh's people, who imposed terrible torment, slaughtered sons, and spared women, showing the bodily reality of oppressive mastery.
The same rescue formula recalls Pharaoh's slaughter and humiliation, making deliverance an escape from the hard tyrannical hand.
Moses reminds Israel that divine favor rescued them from Pharaoh's degrading violence, explicitly setting blessing against oppression.
The angels over the Fire are described as harsh and stern and never disobey God, a divinely assigned context where hardness serves judgment rather than ego.
Believers are commanded to fight nearby hostile forces and let them find firmness in them, another contextual boundary to generalized softness.
The infant Moses is cast into the chest and river, taken by an enemy, yet covered with divine love and formed under God's eye; a dangerous “casting away” becomes preserving care.
Moses' sister leads to a caregiver, and God returns him to his mother so her eyes may be comforted, completing the infant's sheltered recovery.
Moses' mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river only when afraid, and neither fear nor grieve because God will return him; tenderness and trust frame the release.
Pharaoh's household picks up the infant who will become their enemy, identifying the threatening house into which the vulnerable child is received.
Pharaoh's wife says “Do not kill him” and proposes benefit or adoption, a gentle protective intervention inside the tyrant's household.
When Moses refuses other nurses, his sister guides the household to a family who will care for him sincerely, supplying the practical shelter he needs.
God returns Moses to his mother so her eye is comforted and she no longer grieves, fulfilling the soft promise of 28:7.
The Egyptian who buys Joseph tells his wife to honor his lodging and considers adopting him, turning a trafficked child toward household shelter.
When Joseph reaches maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the preservation begun by his honored lodging in 12:21.
Jonah is cast onto the bare shore while sick, the exposed condition that divine favor in 68:49 prevents from becoming blameworthy abandonment.
God grows a spreading gourd over Jonah, adding bodily shade and shelter to the exposed shore scene of 37:145.
Amid battlefield flight, God sends His sakīnah upon the Messenger and believers before divine forces reverse the defeat; calm meets the source dictionary's defeated haste.
Spouses are created so one may find tranquility with the other, and affection and mercy are placed between them; a close human bond is defined by gentle repose.
Humanity is created from one soul with its mate so that he may find rest with her, another relational form of the section's stillness.
God makes homes places of rest and livestock hides into light, portable dwellings, concretizing shelter, ease, and compliant animals in one provision scene.
عَطَاءً حِسَابًا names the hereafter's ample recompense as a gift from the Lord, another direct occurrence of the section's giving root.
By the Lord's blessing, the Prophet is not mad; divine niʿmah directly answers a degrading verbal accusation aimed at him.
Whatever blessing people possess is from God, locating the section's named niʿmah root wholly in divine provision.
God has lavished apparent and hidden favors upon people, broadening the named blessing root from visible ease to unseen care.
Lot wishes for power or refuge in a strong support against the mob; the shelter root here names the secure backing sought under imminent coercion.
When marriage ends before consummation, women are to be provided for and released graciously, another gentle rule for letting go rather than retaining control.
The Prophet is commanded to exercise beautiful patience, a composed response to pressure consistent with the section's calm bearing.
Joseph's brothers arrive in distress with poor merchandise and ask him to give full measure and be charitable, a concrete scene of vulnerable petition.
Joseph answers the brothers who once harmed him with “No blame upon you today” and prayer for forgiveness, the petition scene's strikingly gentle resolution.
God hears the woman who pleads with the Prophet and complains to Him, giving a vulnerable speaker divine attention rather than rebuke.
When servants ask about God, He answers that He is near and responds to the caller who calls, making attentive reception the divine answer to asking.
“Call upon Me; I will answer you” positively invites petition, the opposite of meeting the asker with verbal rejection.
God is the One who answers the distressed caller and removes harm, turning supplication into relief rather than humiliation.
